questions.question: A student draws 20 ml of air into a syringe and seals the tip. When the plunger is pushed down, the air is compressed to 10 ml. What happens to the MASS of the air?
questions.explanation: Compressing air reduces its VOLUME but does NOT change its MASS. The same amount of air particles are now packed into a smaller space. Mass is the amount of matter, and no air was added or removed.

questions.question: Using the same syringe from the previous question (20 ml compressed to 10 ml), what happens to the VOLUME of the air?
options: Volume cannot be measured for gases
questions.explanation: When the plunger is pushed down, the air particles are forced closer together. This reduces the space they occupy, so the VOLUME decreases from 20 ml to 10 ml. Gases can be compressed because their particles have large spaces between them.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the properties of the three states of matter?
options: Solid: definite shape and volume; Liquid: definite volume but no definite shape; Gas: no definite shape or volume
Solid: no definite shape; Liquid: definite shape; Gas: definite volume
Solid: no definite volume; Liquid: no definite shape; Gas: definite shape
Solid: definite volume only; Liquid: definite shape only; Gas: both definite
questions.explanation: Solids keep their shape and size. Liquids take the shape of their container but have a fixed amount (volume). Gases spread out to fill any container—they have no fixed shape or size.

questions.question: A jar is completely filled with large marbles. When rice is poured in, the rice fills the spaces between the marbles without overflowing the jar. Why is this possible?
options: The marbles shrink to make space
Air spaces exist between the marbles, and the smaller rice grains fill these gaps
Rice is a liquid that flows into empty spaces
The jar magically expands to hold more
questions.explanation: Solid objects like marbles do not pack perfectly—air occupies the gaps between them. Smaller solid particles (rice) can fit into these air spaces, allowing more matter to be packed into the same container volume.

questions.question: A student places an empty cup upside down and pushes it straight down into a basin of water. Water does NOT enter the cup. What does this show?
options: Air occupies space and blocks the water from entering
questions.explanation: The cup is not empty—it contains air. Air is matter that occupies space. When pushed underwater, the trapped air fills the cup's space and prevents water from entering. This proves air takes up space.

questions.question: Continuing from the previous question: When the student tilts the upside-down cup slightly underwater, bubbles rise and water enters the cup. What does this show?
options: Air can be pushed out of a space, allowing water to take its place
questions.explanation: Tilting the cup gives the trapped air a path to escape (seen as bubbles rising). Once the air leaves, its space becomes available, and water flows in to occupy that space. This shows that two types of matter cannot occupy the same space at the same time.

questions.question: A deflated balloon is placed on a balance and shows a mass of 3 grams. After inflating it with air, the mass reads 3.5 grams. What does this prove?
questions.explanation: The inflated balloon weighs more because air was added. Since mass increased, air must have mass. This proves air (a gas) is matter.

questions.question: Which of these can be easily compressed (reduced in volume) by pushing?
questions.explanation: Gases like air can be compressed because their particles are far apart with empty space between them. Solids (wood, metal) and liquids (water) have particles packed closely together and cannot be compressed easily.

questions.question: A student pours sand into a measuring cup until it is full. After tapping the cup gently on the table, more sand can be added. Why?
options: Tapping removes air, making the sand disappear
Tapping allows sand grains to settle closer together, reducing air spaces between them
questions.explanation: Dry sand grains have irregular shapes and do not pack perfectly—air fills the gaps. Tapping makes the grains rearrange into a tighter arrangement, reducing the air spaces. This creates room for more sand to be added.

questions.question: A plastic bottle is half-filled with water and tightly capped. When squeezed, the bottle deforms but the water level does not drop. What does this show about liquids?
options: Liquids cannot be compressed—their volume stays constant
Water turns into gas when squeezed
questions.explanation: Unlike gases, liquids have particles packed closely together with little space between them. Squeezing cannot significantly reduce this space, so the water's volume stays the same. The bottle deforms instead.

questions.question: Which container holds matter that has NO definite shape AND NO definite volume?
options: A ice cube in a tray
questions.explanation: Air (a gas) takes the shape of its container and expands to fill all available space. It has no fixed shape or volume. Solids (ice, rice) have both definite shape and volume. Liquids (juice) have definite volume but no definite shape.

questions.question: A student has two identical sealed plastic bags. Bag X contains only air. Bag Y contains air plus a handful of dried beans. Which statement is TRUE?
options: Bag X has more mass because air is heavy
Bag Y has more mass because it contains more matter (air + beans)
Both bags have the same mass because the bags are identical
Bag X has no mass because air is 'nothing'
questions.explanation: Mass is the amount of matter. Bag Y contains all the air that Bag X has PLUS the beans. More matter = more mass. This shows that both solids (beans) and gases (air) contribute to mass.

questions.question: When a stone is lowered into a full cup of water, water spills out. Why?
options: The stone absorbs water and releases it
The stone occupies space, pushing out an equal volume of water
questions.explanation: Matter occupies space. The stone takes up space inside the cup, so the water that was in that space must move out. The spilled water volume equals the stone's volume—this is called displacement.

questions.question: A sponge feels light and can be squeezed flat. A rock of the same size feels heavy and cannot be squeezed. What is the main reason?
options: Sponges are made of magic material
Sponges contain many air spaces that can be reduced when squeezed; rocks have almost no air spaces
Rocks are alive and resist squeezing
questions.explanation: A sponge has a porous structure filled with air pockets. Squeezing pushes the air out and reduces these spaces, decreasing volume. A rock has a compact structure with minimal air spaces, so its volume cannot be reduced by squeezing.

questions.question: Which activity BEST shows that air occupies space?
options: Watching clouds move in the sky
Blowing up a balloon until it expands
questions.explanation: As you blow air into a balloon, it expands because the added air occupies space inside. The more air added, the more space it takes up, making the balloon larger. This directly shows air is matter that occupies space.
